notes:
**Windows** — run `ruze_0.0.25_x64-setup.exe`.
**Linux** — `flatpak install ruze-0.0.25.flatpak`, then `flatpak run com.ruze.chat`.
**Android** — sideload `ruze-0.0.25.apk`. arm64 devices, Android 8.0 or newer.

---

### Added

- **Double-click a voice channel to be in it.** One click opens the room and
  shows you who is there; two puts you in it, without going for the Join
  button. The channel you are actually in is marked in the list, which is not
  always the one you are looking at.

- **Pin the friends window to a corner.** It is the window you leave open
  beside everything else, and putting it back in its corner was a small chore
  every time it opened. Choose a corner from its title bar — the picker is four
  quadrants of a screen — and it goes there, this launch and every one after.
  It sits two pixels off the corner of the work area — against the edge
  without touching it, and never behind the taskbar.

- **Light and dark, and a colour of your own.** Ruze has always had both
  palettes and always followed the desktop's, with no way to disagree with it.
  Settings → Appearance now offers all three answers — match the system, light,
  dark — and remembers which. Beside them, the accent: the colour of a filled
  button, the channel you are in, a link, a name. Eleven to pick from, and the
  text version of whichever you choose is worked out for the theme you are in,
  so it stays readable on white and on black.

- **The side panels can be dragged to any width you like.** The channel list,
  the friends list and the member list each have a seam you can pull, and the
  conversation takes whatever is left. Double-click a seam to put it back where
  it was, or move it with the arrow keys once it has focus. Each width is
  remembered on this device — a laptop and a desktop signed into the same
  account are allowed to disagree about it.

### Changed

- **Nobody home.** An empty connection graph used to be a sentence where the
  picture should be. It now draws the graph honestly — you, a line going out,
  and nothing on the end of it — with your node still pinging into the dark.

- **A constellation beside your name, and one door behind it.** The three
  bars next to your name were a signal meter, which is the wrong picture twice
  over — there are no bars of strength in a peer-to-peer network, and what is
  behind the button is a graph. It is a node with three others around it now,
  with a signal running out along each link, and it is the only way into
  Connections: the dot by the server name went back to being an indicator.

- **One Connections dialog, in two pages.** Whether this device is reachable
  and who you can actually reach were two separate dialogs, each opened from
  the place that implied the other one: the server's name showed you your own
  UDP sockets, and the pulse beside your name showed you other people. They are
  one dialog now — People and This device — and it opens from the pulse, which
  is the light both were about. Opened from a server it shows that server's
  people; the relay setting it used to carry a second copy of stays in
  Settings.

- **Everything about a server is under its name.** Inviting people and making
  a channel were two icons at the foot of the channel list — a long way from
  the thing they act on, and a pair of glyphs to learn. The server name at the
  top is now a menu: create a channel, invite people, server settings,
  connection health, in words.

- **The scrollbars belong to the app now.** They were the operating system's,
  which on a black window meant a pale grey slab down the edge of every list.
  They are thin, rounded and drawn in the theme's own ink — and still as wide
  to grab as they ever were, which is the part thin scrollbars usually get
  wrong.

- **A popped-out conversation is named after the person in it**, in its title
  bar and in the taskbar — where all of them used to be called Ruze, which is
  no help at all when three are open.

- **The title bar says which server you are in**, with its icon beside the
  name, and stays reachable with a dialog open — dragging the window, and the
  three buttons, work whatever is on screen.

- **The interface is sized in rem now.** Every size in the app was a pixel
  count, which meant nothing could grow together: text, spacing, avatars and
  icons were each pinned to a number. They are all fractions of one root size,
  and that root is the usual sixteen pixels. Nothing looks different today —
  every value was converted to the size it already was — but the whole
  interface can now be scaled by changing one line rather than fifteen hundred.

- **Ruze draws its own title bar.** The window had the desktop's bar across
  the top — a strip of somebody else's grey above a black app, with its own
  idea of the theme and no way to be told otherwise. It is the app's now, in
  the app's colours, with the minimize, maximize and close buttons where
  Windows puts them and at the size Windows makes them. Drag it, or
  double-click it to maximize.

- **Your status sits on your picture.** It was a separate dot along the row,
  which is a control nobody reads as being about the face beside it. It is a
  badge on the corner of the avatar now, where everybody else's is, and still
  opens the same menu.

- **Your profile floats at the bottom left.** It was the last row of the
  channel list, which meant it belonged to whichever column happened to be on
  screen and moved about as those columns changed. It is a card of its own now,
  pinned to the foot of the window over the list beside it, and it stays where
  it is while that list scrolls.

- **Settings shows one section at a time.** It was a single column with every
  setting stacked in it, so finding the one you came in for meant scrolling
  past the rest and the list beside it was a set of bookmarks into a page.
  Choosing a heading now draws that section and only that section. The search
  still narrows the list, and the dialog stays the size it was so the panel
  does not resize under you as you move between them.

- **A conversation looks like a channel now.** Direct messages were drawn as
  bubbles down alternating sides with the time in the gutter, and channels as a
  row with your picture, your name and the time along the top. Same act, two
  layouts, each with its own reactions, its own emoji handling and its own
  everything. It is one layout — the channel's — so your picture, the name and
  the timestamp are in the same place wherever you are reading.

- **A conversation uses the same message box as a channel.** It had a plain
  input with a Send button beside it while channels had the rounded box with
  the attach, emoji and GIF controls in it — two boxes for one act, drifting
  apart with every change to either. There is one box now, and it knows which
  of the two it is writing to.

- **The delivery mark is a mark again.** A message nobody has synced with you
  yet said so in words, in the middle of the conversation, on every message it
  was true of. It is a small clock beside the time now, and says what it means
  when you hover or focus it.

### Fixed

- **The bottom of the app is on the screen again on a phone.** The message box,
  the Send button and the bar with your name on it were below the fold: they
  existed, but reaching them meant scrolling the whole app up, and scrolling
  back to read anything. A column in a long channel — or a server with more
  channels than fit, or a busy voice room — grew to the height of its contents
  instead of scrolling inside itself, and took whatever sat beneath it off the
  bottom of the screen.

  The page is now exactly the window and never taller, so nothing can hide
  under the edge of it; the lists scroll, and the things you press stay put.
  The two screens that genuinely can be taller than a phone — the welcome
  screen with its advanced sections open, and the join screen — scroll
  themselves, and no longer centre their contents so hard that the top is cut
  off when they do.

  Every bar that ought to stay put now says so: the composer, the user bar, the
  call bar, the voice controls, and the headers above a list. And the server
  rail scrolls only its servers, so joining one server too many can no longer
  push Friends off the top or Settings off the bottom.

- **Your picture shows in the friends window.** It was drawing your initials
  even when you had one, because it was looking for your face in the cache
  kept for everybody else's.

- **No invitation to a server somebody is already in.** Opening a friend's card
  offered to invite them into every server you run, including the ones you are
  both standing in. It now offers the ones they are not in, which on a card
  whose whole job is to say where somebody is was the least it could do.
